title: Justice against yourselves
hookLine: stand firm for justice even against yourselves, parents or kin (4:135)
tomorrow: Peace between the two is better
last: ADD THE MERCY AND THE BLESSINGS.

cards: It's easy to be fair about strangers. It's harder about your brother.
When your own kid is in the playground fight, when your parent cut in line, when your company fudged the numbers, the mind gets very creative very fast. Suddenly there's context. There were reasons.
The other side started it. An-Nisa has a verse that goes straight for that blind spot and names it out loud.

teach.h: QAWWAMIN: STANDING UP, AGAIN AND AGAIN
teach.b: In Pickthall's words, 4:135 says: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred."
Rich or poor, the verse goes on, God is nearer to both than you are. So don't follow your desires and swerve from justice.
The Arabic for staunch, qawwamin, is an intensive form: not people who are fair once, but people who keep standing up for justice, again and again.
And at the end, the verb ta'dilu, from 'adl, justice: being level, like two pans of a scale at rest. Look at the order.
Then parents, whom the Qur'an elsewhere tells people to honor. Then relatives. Honoring your parents, the verse implies, never means lying for them.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari shows the Prophet ﷺ holding to this. A woman from a powerful Meccan clan was caught stealing, and her family sent someone the Prophet loved to ask for her to be let off.
He was angry, and said peoples before them had been ruined because they let the powerful go and punished the weak.
Then he named his own family: even if it were Fatimah, his own daughter, the law would be the same.

teach.h: EVEN THOUGH IT BE AGAINST YOURSELVES.
teach.b: So this week ends where it began: kindness at home, burdens carried lightly, the near neighbor and the far, trusts returned, disputes referred back, greetings answered with better.
And now the one that turns the mirror around: justice that starts with me.

how: Muslims hold 'adl, justice, as a central duty, and 4:135 is quoted by judges, scholars and activists to insist that testimony and judgment must be honest even against oneself and one's family.

o: revenge equal to the harm that was done
a ruling handed down by a judge
justice: level, like a balanced scale

games.q: justice against yourselves — tap the pairs.
p: justice: level, like a balanced scale
standing up for it again and again
named in the hadith of the thief

s: the verse makes an exception for parents
parents are on the list: justice even against them.
people who keep standing up for justice, not just once.
the Prophet let a noble woman off because her clan was powerful
Bukhari reports he refused, warning that favoring the powerful ruined peoples before.

games.q: a powerful family sends someone the Prophet loves to ask him to let their daughter off for theft. what does he say?
o: he agrees, to keep the peace.
even if it were Fatimah, my daughter, the law would be the same.
he sends the case to someone else.
games.why: he named his own daughter, and warned that peoples were ruined for letting the powerful go and punishing the weak.

practice: Think of a recent conflict where you were part of the problem, maybe not the whole problem, but part.
Picture it as an honest witness would, without defending yourself, and find one plain sentence of admission: I was unfair about that. I see it now.

wordCard.voice: 'Adl. Justice: being level, like a balanced scale, even against yourself, your parents or your kin, from 4:135. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: justice, balance; 4:135 uses the verb ta'dilu, to be just, to keep level.

carryVoice: Your line: justice, even against me. Yourselves first, then parents, then kin. And that's a week.
